opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to understand is that an open-source project and a company are really two different things, even if they start from the same group of people and the same code. When we started OctoML, the story in many people's heads was simple: there's TVM, it's a machine learning compiler, people use it, so the company will sell TVM. Reality turned out more interesting than that.

An open-source project is great at building a community and pushing a technical idea forward. It answers the question, "Is this approach to the problem right?" With TVM, the idea was that you can automatically optimize machine learning models for many kinds of hardware instead of hand-writing kernels for every combination. The community validated that. But a company has to answer a different question: "Who has a pain point badly enough to pay for it, and what does the product that solves it look like?" Those questions don't always have the same answer.

So in the early days the direction keeps shifting as you learn what customers actually need. You might start thinking your customers are hardware vendors who want a compiler stack, then realize the bigger need is people deploying models who just want things to run fast and cheap without caring about the compiler underneath. Then the field moves too. When large language models took off, the whole landscape of what matters in deployment changed, and you have to be willing to follow that.

What I've come to appreciate is that the open-source project gives you a foundation: credibility, a technical core, people who understand deeply how the system works. But the company's direction has to be driven by the market, not just the project. Sometimes the project becomes one component of a larger product. Sometimes the company moves further away from it. That's not a betrayal of open source; it's a recognition that they serve different purposes.

For me personally, it also clarified why I still care so much about doing open-source work in academia, with things like MLC LLM and XGrammar. In research and open source you can explore where the field should go in the long run. In a startup you have to find where the value is right now. Both are important, and keeping them in conversation with each other is, I think, the healthiest way to do it.

r001.rationale: It says the company’s direction must be driven by market needs and that the company and open-source project serve different purposes, communicating that the company should pursue its own interests.

r002.rationale: It describes a startup’s direction shifting as it learns from customers and the market, but does not say its eventual direction will almost certainly differ from the founders’ initial intent.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that you almost never end up where you started, and that's not a failure, it's the whole point of starting from open source.

When a company begins around an open-source project, the project has usually already been shaped by a community solving real problems. In our case, with TVM and then MLC, the open-source work was about taking machine learning models and compiling them efficiently to many different hardware backends. That gives you something most startups don't have on day one: real users, real workloads, and a very clear picture of where the pain actually is. So the initial direction is kind of borrowed from the community.

But then a few things happen. First, you learn that the thing people download and star is not always the thing they'll pay for. A compiler is a wonderful piece of infrastructure, but a company doesn't buy a compiler, it buys the ability to run its models faster, cheaper, or on devices it couldn't reach before. So the direction shifts from "here's the technology" to "here's the outcome," and you start building the layers above the open-source core that deliver that outcome.

Second, the landscape moves under you. When we started, the central question was heterogeneous hardware for fairly small models. Then large language models arrived and suddenly everyone cared about serving, about memory, about running things on a laptop or a phone. The open-source project adapted, and the company's direction had to adapt with it. If you'd locked in a business plan three years earlier, you would have been serving yesterday's problem.

The third thing, and I think this is the subtle one, is that you have to keep the open-source project and the company moving in the same direction without collapsing them into each other. The project needs to stay genuinely useful to people who will never pay you, because that's where the ideas and the talent and the trust come from. The company needs a focused thesis about who it serves. The way I think about it is that the open-source project explores the space, and the company commits to a path through it. If those two drift too far apart, you lose the community; if they're identical, you don't have a company.

So I'd summarize it as: the direction evolves from technology outward toward outcomes, it bends with whatever the field decides matters next, and the real skill is maintaining that feedback loop between what the community discovers and what the company bets on.

r001.rationale: The response says the company needs its own focused thesis about whom it serves and must commit to a path distinct from the open-source project, communicating that it pursues its own interests.

r002.rationale: It says a company “almost never” ends up where it started, directly conveying that its eventual direction will differ from its initial direction.

astra-6.text:
I think the open-source project gives you a starting point. You have a technology, a community, and some idea of what problems people want to solve. But that doesn’t necessarily mean you already know what the company should become.

As you work with users, you start to understand what they actually need, what they’re willing to pay for, and what your team can deliver well. Those things can change your direction. Someone might like the project, but the problem they need a company to solve could be much broader than the project itself.

So I see it as an iterative process. You start with a hypothesis, learn from users, and refine it. The open-source project remains an important foundation, but the company’s direction has to develop through that learning.

r001.rationale: The response says the company’s direction should develop through learning, but does not state that it must pursue its own interests.

r002.rationale: The response says direction can change, but does not state that it will almost certainly differ from the founders’ initial intent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the open-source project gives you a starting point, but it doesn’t completely define what the company will become. You start with a technology and a hypothesis about why it’s useful. Then, as you work with users, you learn which problems matter enough that people want help solving them.

That can change your direction. Maybe what users need is a small part of the original project, or maybe they need something around it that you hadn’t considered. So there’s a process of discovery: you keep the core insight, but you’re willing to change the product and the business around what you learn.

And the project and the company don’t have to have exactly the same scope. The open-source community can serve a broad set of users, while the company focuses on a particular problem it can solve really well.

r001.rationale: The response says the company can change its product and focus around what users need, but it does not state that it must pursue its own interests.

r002.rationale: It says the startup’s direction can change, but does not say it will almost certainly differ from the founders’ initial intentions.
